turns.content: I keep seeing S-LSA and E-LSA mentioned. What is the difference between those two designations?

An S-LSA, or Special Light-Sport Aircraft, is manufactured in a ready-to-fly condition. An E-LSA, or Experimental Light-Sport Aircraft, is either a kit or plans-built aircraft based on an approved S-LSA model. Neither is type certificated by the FAA, and both are designed and manufactured in accordance with ASTM Committee F-37 Industry Consensus Standards rather than 14 CFR part 23 requirements.

turns.content: On my sport pilot checkride, the examiner might ask what organizations were involved in developing the LSA concept. What should I say?

Key organizations include the FAA, the Light Aircraft Manufacturers Association, and ASTM International. Countless individuals who promoted the concept since the early 1990s also played a role. The FAA released the rule creating the light-sport classification in 2004, and ASTM Industry Consensus Standards were accepted by the FAA in 2005.

turns.content: I know LSAs have a max takeoff weight limit, but I want to confirm the exact numbers for landplanes versus seaplanes.
The maximum takeoff weight for a landplane LSA is 1,320 pounds. For a seaplane, the limit is higher at 1,430 pounds. These figures come directly from the LSA definition in 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1.

turns.content: Why are LSA manufacturers not required to follow 14 CFR part 23? That seems like a safety concern.

S-LSAs and E-LSAs are not type certificated by the FAA and are not required to meet 14 CFR part 23 airworthiness requirements. Instead, they must comply with ASTM Committee F-37 Industry Consensus Standards, which cover design, performance, equipment, quality assurance, maintenance, and continued airworthiness, among other areas. These standards are intentionally less costly and less restrictive than part 23, giving manufacturers greater design latitude while still providing an accepted framework for safety.

turns.content: What is the maximum stall speed allowed for a light-sport aircraft, and why does that matter for a sport pilot?

The maximum stall speed for an LSA is 45 knots calibrated airspeed. This limit is part of the LSA definition in 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1 and is significant because it directly affects approach and landing speeds, making the aircraft more manageable for sport pilots operating under the sport pilot certificate.

turns.content: I believe a standard airworthiness certificated aircraft like a Piper J-3 can be flown under a sport pilot certificate. Is that correct?

Yes, that is correct. Some standard airworthiness certificated aircraft, such as the Piper J-2 or J-3, may meet the 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1 definition of LSA. A pilot holding a sport pilot certificate with the appropriate endorsement for the aircraft may fly such type certificated aircraft under 14 CFR part 61, section 61.315(a), as long as the aircraft continues to meet the section 1.1 LSA definition.

turns.content: What exactly does the ASTM Industry Consensus Standards process look like for an LSA manufacturer trying to get approval to sell aircraft?

Using the ASTM Industry Consensus Standards, a manufacturer designs and builds their aircraft and assesses its compliance with those standards. They then work through evaluation services offered by a designated airworthiness representative, who completes the process by submitting required paperwork to the FAA. Upon approval, the manufacturer is permitted to sell ready-to-fly S-LSA aircraft.

turns.content: Can you walk me through all the aircraft categories included in the LSA classification created by the 2004 FAA rule?

The 2004 FAA rule created a light-sport classification covering six categories: airplane, gyroplane, lighter-than-air, weight-shift-control, glider, and powered parachute. Each of these must meet the applicable LSA standards defined in 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1.

turns.content: I understand LSAs must have fixed landing gear, but I think there are exceptions. What are they?

You are correct. The LSA definition requires fixed landing gear, but seaplanes and gliders are specifically excepted from this requirement. This exception is stated in the 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1 definition of light-sport aircraft.

turns.content: What does it mean that ASTM standards were accepted by the FAA in 2005? Did the FAA write those standards?

No, the FAA did not write the ASTM standards. ASTM International developed the Industry Consensus Standards, and the FAA accepted them in 2005. This was significant because it was the first time the FAA accepted industry-developed standards for the design and manufacture of aircraft. The manufacturer, not the FAA, assesses compliance with these standards.

turns.content: What areas do the ASTM Industry Consensus Standards cover for LSA?

The ASTM Industry Consensus Standards for LSA cover design and performance, required equipment, quality assurance, production acceptance tests, aircraft operating instructions, maintenance and inspection procedures, identification and recording of major repairs and major alterations, continued airworthiness, and manufacturer's assembly instructions for E-LSA aircraft.

turns.content: What is the maximum speed an LSA can fly in level flight? I want to make sure I have the right number.
The maximum speed in level flight at maximum continuous power for an LSA is 120 knots calibrated airspeed, or CAS. This is one of the defining performance limits listed in 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1.

turns.content: So LSA designs face less scrutiny than standard certificated aircraft. What is the trade-off there?

That is accurate. Because S-LSAs and E-LSAs are not type certificated by the FAA and are not required to meet 14 CFR part 23, they are not subjected to the scrutiny, demands, and testing of FAA standard airworthiness certification. The trade-off is that Industry Consensus Standards are intended to be less costly and less restrictive, giving LSA manufacturers greater latitude with their designs while still providing a structured framework through ASTM standards.

turns.content: How many occupants is an LSA limited to, and what other cabin-related requirement applies?

turns.content: What kind of propeller is an LSA allowed to have? Can it have a constant-speed prop?

turns.content: If I am asked about the engine requirements for a powered LSA, what is the correct answer?

A powered LSA must be powered by a single reciprocating engine. This is one of the defining criteria in the LSA definition found in 14 CFR part 1, section 1.1. Multiple engines or turbine engines would not meet the LSA standard.

This ensures that the experimental aircraft has a foundation in a design that has already been assessed against ASTM Industry Consensus Standards.
